h1:
Hat Yai Shopping
Malls, Markets & Souvenirs by District
intro: Hat Yai has been a shopping town for as long as anyone can remember. Southern Thais and visitors driving over from Malaysia and Singapore come here to shop as a matter of routine. The appeal is that air-conditioned malls and old street markets sit close enough to walk between in one afternoon. This guide takes you through it district by district — Central Festival, Lee Gardens, Kim Yong Market, Santisuk Market and the Niphat Uthit strip — and closes with the souvenirs Hat Yai locals actually buy.

blocks.html: When people say "you have to shop in Hat Yai," they really mean several districts that sit very close together. The old town core is almost all walkable, while the big malls are just outside the center but easy to reach by songthaew (shared pickup truck). We'll start with the malls, then head down to the old markets that are the real heart of Hat Yai shopping.

blocks.text: Central Festival Hat Yai — the biggest mall in the South

blocks.html: Central Festival Hat Yai opened in late 2013 and is still the largest mall in southern Thailand. It sits on Kanchanawanit Road in the Kho Hong area, about 3–4 km from the city center. Inside you'll find easy-to-find brands like Uniqlo and H&M, plus a Robinson department store, a supermarket, a cinema, and a top-floor dining zone with nice city views in the early evening. It's a good place to escape the afternoon heat and roll straight into dinner.

items: Address — 1518 Kanchanawanit Rd, Kho Hong, Hat Yai, Songkhla
Getting there — Take a Phetkasem-line songthaew, fare around 10–15 THB. There's a footbridge from the Makro side that leads straight into the mall.
Good for — Mainstream fashion brands, food court, cinema, plenty of parking

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: If you're traveling as a group and have a car, parking at Central is far easier than parking in the old town. Finish the Kim Yong and Santisuk markets before evening, then drive to Central for dinner and a movie.

blocks.text: Lee Gardens Plaza — the landmark tower in the city center

blocks.html: Before Central arrived, Lee Gardens Plaza was the shopping and accommodation hub of Hat Yai. The tall tower is a city-center landmark you can spot from a distance. It's quieter than Central these days, but the location is excellent because it sits right next to the market district — a few steps from the building and you're at Kim Yong and Santisuk. The lower floors still have shops and restaurants, so it works well as a base for shopping the old town on foot.

items: Location — Old-town core, on Saneha Nuson / Prachathipat Rd, walkable to the markets
Why it helps — An easy-to-find meeting point and a starting hub for walking the city
Good for — People staying nearby who want to shop on foot without taking a songthaew

blocks.text: Kim Yong Market — souvenir and import heaven

blocks.html: If you only have time for one place, make it Kim Yong. This is a two-floor covered market on Niphat Uthit 3 Road that locals and visitors alike rate as Hat Yai's number-one souvenir spot. It's open from morning to evening. The ground floor is food — nuts, dried fruit, Malaysian and Singaporean snacks — while the upper floor has electronics, toys and all sorts of imported goods.

Inside it's divided into several lanes, so your first walk through can feel a little confusing. The trick is to focus on one category at a time: start with dried seafood like squid and dried shrimp, which is usually cheaper than buying at a mall, then move on to nuts and snacks sold by weight, and finish with the imported sweets.

items: Dried seafood — Dried squid, dried shrimp, salted fish; better prices than the malls, and you can haggle if you buy a lot
Nuts and snacks — Cashews, fried beans, sold by weight; several stalls let you taste before you buy
Imported sweets — Chocolate, biscuits, Malaysian and Singaporean snacks on the second floor, cheaper than in Bangkok

blocks.title: Tips for Kim Yong
blocks.html: For anything sold by weight, compare 2–3 stalls before you stock up — prices vary a little. And ask whether the price is per kilo or per 100 grams (khit), so there are no surprises when you pay.

blocks.text: Santisuk Market — fashion, bags, perfume, bargains

blocks.html: A short walk on from Kim Yong brings you to Santisuk Market, another long-running market that's a legend among shoppers. Its strength is budget fashion and everyday goods — clothes, leather goods, bags, shoes, sunglasses, perfume and cosmetics. There are well over a hundred stalls, and it's open roughly 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

items: Fashion — Clothes, shoulder bags, luggage, leather shoes, with low starting prices
Beauty — Perfume and cosmetics in many brands, cheaper than a mall counter
Odds and ends — Hiking gear, flashlights, kids' toys, small electronics

blocks.title: Buy cheap, but stay sharp
blocks.html: With some cheap items the quality matches the price, especially knock-off brands. Check the material and stitching before you pay, and inspect everything as you receive it, because many stalls make returns or exchanges difficult.

blocks.text: Niphat Uthit 1-2-3 — the commercial heart of Hat Yai

blocks.html: Niphat Uthit Roads 1, 2 and 3 are the main arteries of Hat Yai's commercial district. The three run parallel and connect through to one another, and both Kim Yong and Santisuk markets sit within this area. The streets are lined with gold shops, pharmacies, souvenir stores, restaurants and hotels — it's the most enjoyable part of town to explore on foot, and you can find nearly everything by circling these blocks.

items.name: Niphat Uthit 1
items.blurb: Gold shops, souvenir stores and pharmacies in old shophouses that are still busy; walks through to Santisuk

items.name: Niphat Uthit 2
items.blurb: Restaurants, cafes and hotels; the street where many visitors stay, with plenty of food at night

items.name: Niphat Uthit 3
items.blurb: Home of Kim Yong Market, packed with souvenir and import stores the whole length — good for a long shopping stroll

blocks.text: Hat Yai souvenirs worth actually buying

blocks.html: Hat Yai has so many souvenir options it's hard to choose. We've picked only the ones locals genuinely buy and that are easy to carry home, with ballpark prices as of early 2026. Prices shift by shop and season, so use these as a rough guide before you buy.

items.name: Rose pastries (Pia Kularb) from Baan Ko Kai
items.blurb: Layered-pastry sweets shaped like rose petals, from a shop famous across Hat Yai. There are several fillings, both traditional and modern, and it makes an impressive yet easy-to-carry gift.

items.name: Fried bao buns from Ko Uan
items.blurb: A souvenir that regular Hat Yai visitors know well, with red-pork, salted-egg and taro fillings. Buy them frozen and fry them at home, and the shell crisps up like it was just made.

items.name: Cashews (from Kim Yong)
items.blurb: Sold by the kilo in Kim Yong Market, in salted, honey-roasted and sugar-coated versions. Prices beat the malls, and several stalls let you taste before buying.

items.name: Salted fish & dried seafood
items.blurb: Salted fish from Songkhla Lake, dried squid and dried shrimp — all available at Kim Yong at good prices. These are Songkhla specialties southern Thais bring home regularly.

items.name: Fried beans & snacks by weight
items.blurb: Fried beans, peanuts and a range of snacks at Kim Yong, sold by the kilo. Good for splitting among several people or for snacking on the road.
items.price: from a few hundred THB per kilo

items.name: Malaysian & Singaporean imported snacks
items.blurb: Chocolate, biscuits, dried fruit and jerky on the second floor of Kim Yong, cheaper than in the big cities and full of unusual finds you won't see elsewhere.

items.name: Mango leather & candied mango
items.blurb: Processed-fruit sweets with a tart-sweet flavor, sold by several shops in town. Best bought just before you leave, since the fresh kind doesn't keep long.

items.name: Southern curry pastes & chili dips
items.blurb: Southern curry pastes and chili dips in vacuum packs, ready to cook southern food at home. Lightweight and they keep for a long time.

items.name: Bird's nest
items.blurb: A premium gift, with specialist shops like Thai Arun Bird's Nest in town. Good for gifting to elders; prices start in the hundreds and rise by grade, so ask the staff about quality before buying.

blocks.title: What to buy right before you leave
blocks.html: Buy fresh items like candied mango or frozen bao buns close to departure so they don't spoil while you're out and about. Dried goods like salted fish, nuts and curry paste can be bought any day in advance.

If you only have a single day but want to cover it all, run it like this: do the old markets in the morning and early afternoon while it's still bearable to walk, then finish in the cool, air-conditioned mall in the evening.

items.activity: Start at Kim Yong Market on Niphat Uthit 3
items.note: Shop for souvenirs before the crowds build; pick up dried goods and nuts first
Stop at gold shops, souvenir stores and sweet shops along the way
Pick out budget clothes, bags and perfume
Escape the heat, grab a coffee, use it as a break before moving on

items.activity: Take a songthaew to Central Festival

items.note: Finish with a movie or a supermarket run before heading back

faq.q: Where's the best shopping in Hat Yai?
faq.a: It depends on what you're buying. For souvenirs, head to Kim Yong Market; for fashion and bargains, head to Santisuk Market. Both are in the Niphat Uthit district and within walking distance of each other. For mall brands and a cinema, go to Central Festival.

faq.q: What's the difference between Kim Yong and Santisuk markets?
faq.a: Kim Yong focuses on food and souvenirs — nuts, salted fish, imported snacks. Santisuk focuses on fashion — clothes, bags, shoes, perfume and budget cosmetics. The two markets sit close together in the Niphat Uthit district and you can walk straight from one to the other.

faq.q: What are the must-buy Hat Yai souvenirs?
faq.a: The popular ones are rose pastries from Baan Ko Kai, fried bao buns from Ko Uan, cashews, salted fish and dried seafood from Kim Yong, plus Malaysian and Singaporean imported snacks you can find at Kim Yong Market.

faq.q: What time do Hat Yai's markets open?
faq.a: Kim Yong Market is open from morning to evening, while Santisuk Market runs roughly 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Central Festival keeps standard mall hours, about 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

faq.q: How do I get to Central Festival Hat Yai?
faq.a: It's on Kanchanawanit Road in the Kho Hong area, about 3–4 km from the old town. Take a Phetkasem-line songthaew, fare around 10–15 THB. There's a footbridge from the Makro side that leads straight into the mall.
